title: Kaepernick Fires Back at Jerry Jones a Decade Later
htmlContent:
Ten years have passed since Colin Kaepernick first took a knee during the national anthem as quarterback of the San Francisco 49ers. He never returned to the NFL, but he kept fighting. Now, with a new book in hand and a Dallas crowd in front of him, the former signal-caller had a sharp message for Cowboys owner Jerry Jones and the league that moved on without him.

A Pointed Question in Jerry Jones' Backyard

Kaepernick appeared on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at The Black Academy of Arts and Letters in Dallas for an author talk on his memoir and manifesto, The Perilous Fight, presented by The Dock Bookshop. It was a fitting stage, as Jones once threatened to bench any who knelt during the anthem.

Asked what he would say to Jones and others who opposed his protest, Kaepernick did not soften his stance, according to insider Clarence Hill Jr.

"It's the same thing that I've said in the past, which is, why are you so comfortable working against black folks trying to live? I mean, for me, people that worked, and I think this was one of the unique insights that I got in this process. People revealed who they were."

He then framed the protest in its simplest terms.

"We were fighting specifically against police killing black folks. It's amazing to me that there's anybody that's like, 'I'm against that.' And I think the people who came out and fought against it revealed who they were, revealed their intentions. And my question would be, why are you so comfortable with it? And the question for us, collectively. Why are we supporting it?"

Where It All Began

The movement started during the 2016 season, when Kaepernick sat and then knelt during the anthem to protest police brutality and racial injustice against Black Americans. It quickly became one of the most culturally significant moments in NFL history.

"I am not going to stand up to show pride in a flag for a country that oppresses Black people and people of color. To me, this is bigger than football, and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way." — Colin Kaepernick, 2016

Jones and the Owners Push Back

Jones made no secret of where he stood.

"There is no question the league is suffering negative effects from these protests. At all times, if I am anything, I am first and foremost a proponent of making the NFL strong… If all this makes you stronger to represent messages, let's don't do it in a way that tears down the strength of the NFL." — Jerry Jones, 2017

The issue reached the league's highest levels that October, when about 30 owners, players, and executives gathered urgently at the NFL's Park Avenue headquarters. Late Houston Texans ownerBob McNair was blunt, urging players to rein in their teammates.

"You fellas need to ask your compadres, fellas, stop that other business, let's go out and do something that really produces positive results, and we'll help you." — Bob McNair

A Career Cut Short, a Mission Continued

Kaepernick opted out of his contract after the 49ers told him they planned to release him following a 2-14 season. He has not taken an NFL snap since. He later settled a collusion grievance with the league in 2019 and poured his energy into the Know Your Rights Camp, a youth empowerment organization.

His memoir is meant to fill in the gaps.

"I've gotten so many questions about why did I protest, what happened, what led up to it, the details behind the scenes of all of the moments. Not just the protest, but owners in the NFL, the conversations that were happening there, the workout in 2019 and all the things that transpired around that… I think it's especially critical in a moment like this." — Colin Kaepernick, TIME</em> Magazine

Royce White Reignites the Debate

Not everyone sees Kaepernick's legacy the same way. Royce White, the former NBA first-round pick and 2024 Republican U.S. Senate nominee in Minnesota, recently made a provocative comparison in an interview with Brandon "Scoop B" Robinson.

"Kyrie Irving has surpassed Colin Kaepernick in terms of the genuine impact of his public platform." — Royce White

The clip set off a heated exchange on Instagram. Former NBA forward turned author and activist Etan Thomas replied, "It's not a competition." White shot back, "Are you vaccinated?"—a nod to Irving's 2021 refusal of the COVID-19 vaccine, which cost him much of the Brooklyn Nets' season. Activist Mysonne Linen called for unity, but White did not budge.

"Division is a natural consequence of dishonesty." — Royce White<

White, who also questioned why Kaepernick remains a fixture in mainstream media and challenged him to "evolve" his protest, has built his post-basketball identity on bold takes.

A Legacy Still Being Written

The back-and-forth highlights a question that has followed athlete activism for a decade: is impact measured by visibility, by sacrifice, or by results? Ten years later, he is still asking the same question he asked in Dallas, and still waiting for those who opposed him to answer it.
excerpt: Ten years after Colin Kaepernick first took a knee, the former 49ers quarterback appeared in Dallas to promote his memoir "The Perilous Fight" and delivered a pointed challenge to Cowboys owner Jerry Jones and others who opposed his anthem protest against police brutality and racial injustice.
